The question is what we do with the last group.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c221e3059edf6459bc6a85", "tabs": [ "69c22206c7ede1d4fc6a5fa1", "69c0900d385ce2c1be1ae158", "69c09000d8c5e5cbe7c9eca5", "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c085ddd46b33b7eed0d1f7", "69c0a0d2dad175912e825b7b", "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4" ], "main-content": "

There is someone in my building I have been avoiding for about a year. Nothing dramatic happened — no falling out, no confrontation. She said something once that landed wrong, I pulled back, and then the distance became the default. Now when I hear her in the hallway I wait an extra beat before opening my door.

I haven't told anyone this. It sounds small when I say it. But it has been a year.

We all have these people. Not enemies in any dramatic sense — just the ones we've quietly moved to the edge of our attention. The coworker whose emails we answer last. The family member we call only when we have to. The neighbor we've trained ourselves not to see.

Most of us would not describe this as a failure of love. We'd describe it as self-preservation, or discernment, or just the practical reality of limited time and energy. And sometimes that's true.

But then there's the story Jesus told about a man beaten and left on the road. A priest walks by. A Levite — someone who really should have known better — walks by. And then the Samaritan stops. The Samaritan is, by every social calculation of the first century, the person with the most reasons not to. He is the outsider. The other. The one with legitimate grievances of his own.

He stops anyway.

What Jesus is doing in that story is precise. He's not just commending kindness in general. He's identifying the people we've decided are acceptable — and showing that the acceptable people walked on. The one who loved was the one who had every excuse not to.

The one who loved was the one who had every excuse not to.

I keep thinking about my neighbor in the hallway. She is not in my inner circle. She is barely in my middle circle — the people I tolerate, the ones I manage with polite neutrality. She is, if I'm honest, in my outer circle. And the outer circle runs on its own, quietly, without me ever having decided anything.

Jesus seems to say that the outer circle is exactly where this gets real. Not the dramatic enemies, not the people who require a theology of forgiveness. Just the ordinary ones I've stopped paying attention to.

I don't have a resolution on my neighbor. But I stopped waiting an extra beat last week. That's smaller than I'd like it to be. It might be where it starts.
